questions.question: Describe how you would investigate a pair of pliers and a nutcracker to classify them, and state what the investigation shows about where each tool works best.
questions.expected_answer: Find the pivot, the point where the hand applies effort and the point where the load is acted on. For pliers the pivot rivet lies between the handles and the jaws, so they are first class; gripping near the pivot holds far more firmly than at the tips because the load arm is shortest there. For the nutcracker the hinge is at one end, the nut sits just in front of it and the hands press the far ends, so the load is in the middle and it is second class; a nut placed near the hinge cracks easily while one near the handles barely dents.

questions.question: Explain what a linkage with more than one pivot is, give two examples, and state the rule that connects force and movement through a linkage.
questions.expected_answer: A linkage is a set of levers connected by two or more pivots so that movement at one point is passed along and changed, in size or direction, on the way. Examples: a folding clothes airer or scissor lift, where a small movement at the handles becomes a large movement at the far end; a scissor car jack, where a small turning force is multiplied by a screw and then by lever arms to lift a car; the arms of the Jaws of Life. The rule: where the linkage magnifies movement it reduces force, and where it reduces movement it magnifies force.

questions.question: Describe how the syringe drives the jaws of the model rescue device and name three design decisions that affect how well it grips.
questions.expected_answer: Water pushed from one syringe moves the plunger of a second syringe, which pushes a rod; the rod pushes the back ends of two jaw arms that pivot on a pin, so the tips at the front open or close. The three decisions: the position of the pivot pin, close to the tips for a strong grip but a small opening or towards the back for a wide opening but a weak grip; the tightness of the join between rod and arms, since a loose join wastes movement; and the stiffness of the arms, since a bending arm loses force before it reaches the tips, so arms are doubled or folded.
